title: The Replication File: p-Hacking, Preregistration, and Regressive Shrinkage
description: An audit file where the player reviews case files from the replication crisis in social psychology. The player examines original published studies and their replication attempts, identifying potential p-hacking, questionable research practices (Simmons et al., 2011), and the mathematical inevitability of regressive shrinkage in replication effect sizes (Stanley & Spence, 2014). Each case file provides original data, replication data, and researcher degrees of freedom. The player must decide whether the original finding is robust, a false positive, or inflated by selective reporting. The final case requires evaluating a preregistered replication and distinguishing between 'replication failure' due to low power versus actual null effects (Kenny & Judd, 2019).

case_files.player_task: Classify as robust, false positive, or inflated. Note: Stanley & Spence (2014) show that even at true r = 0.30 with reliability 0.70, 99% of replication r values range from 0.03 to 0.46.

case_files.original_effect: d = 0.92 on risk tolerance, N = 42, p < 0.01
case_files.player_task: Identify QRPs: small N, no preregistration, multiple DVs, selective reporting of highest effect. File drawer analysis estimates true effect near zero.

case_files.original_study: social priming of intelligence (Dijksterhuis & van Knippenberg, 1998, Study 1)
case_files.replication_attempt: d = 0.01, N = 325, p = 0.97 (Doyen et al., 2012, plus multi-lab RR)
case_files.player_task: Evaluate construct validity: did the replication actually manipulate the same construct? Fabrigar et al. (2020) caution that failed replications may reflect construct validity issues rather than false positives.

tools: compute expected replication distribution from Stanley & Spence (2014) simulation parameters
flag p-hacking using Simmons et al. (2011) 'three wishes' criteria

title: Cross-Cultural Measurement: Bias, Equivalence, and the Satisfaction with Life Scale
description: A matrix exercise where the player must diagnose and correct sources of bias in cross-cultural measurement. Using Oishi's (2006) comparison of the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) across US and Chinese samples as a template, the player evaluates items for construct bias, method bias, and item bias (Van de Vijver & Tanzer, 2004). The player runs a series of multiple-group confirmatory factor analyses (MG-CFA), testing configural, metric, and scalar invariance. They identify which SWLS items show differential item functioning across cultures and decide whether to retain, modify, or remove them. The matrix reveals how response biasesÔÇöacquiescence, extreme responding, moderacy, reference group effects (Heine et al., 2002)ÔÇödistort cross-cultural comparisons and threaten validity.

measures.scale: Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985)
measures.configural_invariance: RMSEA = 0.06 (acceptable fit, same item structure across groups)
measures.metric_invariance_test: constrain factor loadings one item at a time; compare delta chi-square
measures.results: Items 1-4: non-significant delta chi-square (equivalent). Item 5: delta chi-square = 12.4, p < 0.01 (biased)
measures.item_5_loadings: US = 0.71, China = 0.38 (item not capturing latent construct effectively in Chinese sample)

measures.known_bias: reference group effect: Japanese respondents compare to ingroup, not abstract standards (Heine et al., 2002)

measures.known_issue: extreme responding bias: Russian and Indian samples show higher SD than US and UK samples (Fischer, 2004)

stimulus.player_task: For each scale: (1) assess configural invariance, (2) test metric invariance by constraining factor loadings, (3) identify biased items, (4) decide retain/modify/remove. Score based on correct interpretation of MG-CFA output and recognition of response bias patterns.

title: Design Validator: Internal, External, Construct, and Statistical Conclusion Validity
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player inspects research designs and scrubs across four validity dimensionsÔÇöinternal, external, construct, and statistical conclusion (Brewer & Crano; Cook & Campbell, 1979)ÔÇöto identify threats. Each research scenario presents a study abstract; the player must adjust design parameters (random assignment, measurement timing, sample characteristics, operational definitions) and observe how each threat (history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, selection, mortality, diffusion) shifts across the four validity types. The station uses real published studies as case material. The goal is to understand the inherent trade-off: strengthening internal validity (lab experiments) often weakens external validity (generalizability), and vice versa (field studies).

scrubbable_design_parameters.trade_off: may reduce external validity if strict inclusion criteria

scrubbable_design_parameters.threats_controlled: history, maturation - longer interval increases maturation risk

scrubbable_design_parameters.threats_reduced: WEIRD bias (Henrich et al., 2010) - college vs. community vs. cross-cultural
construct validity - narrow ops increase construct under-coverage

research_scenarios.scenario: Lab study: effect of mood induction on helping behavior
research_scenarios.player_task: Add cover story to reduce demand (improves internal); add community sample and multiple measures (improves external)

research_scenarios.scenario: Field study: effect of neighborhood disorder on mental health
research_scenarios.player_task: Add propensity score matching to address selection; which validity improves? (Internal, with potential external cost if matching selects unrepresentative subset)

title: Experimental Design: Conquering Confounds
description: A boss battle where the player must design and defend a multi-factorial experiment against a series of validity threats. The player chooses the design type (between-subjects, within-subjects, mixed factorial), assigns factors and levels, and selects counterbalancing strategies. Each design choice reduces some threats but introduces new ones. The 'boss' is a set of progressively harder research questions (from simple attitude change to complex social interaction dynamics) where the player must achieve high internal and construct validity simultaneously. The final battle requires designing a replication-robust experiment that accounts for heterogeneity of variance and nonindependence in dyadic data (Kenny & Judd, 2019). Feedback provides meta-analytic norms for typical effect sizes to inform power analysis.

boss_levels.win_condition: select appropriate counterbalancing and show 3-month follow-up retention rate > 70%

boss_levels.research_question: Does mimicry increase rapport in cross-cultural dyads?
boss_levels.design_recommendation: 2 x 2 x 2 between-subjects with dyadic nonindependence correction
threats_to_manage: nonindependence of dyad members (Kenny et al., Ch23)
cultural response bias in rapport measurement (Ch5)
boss_levels.win_condition: correctly specify APIM model and power analysis accounting for ICC > 0

title: Survey Design Lab: Question Wording, Context Effects, and Response Biases
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player starts with a research question and builds survey items, scrubbing parameters like question wording, response scale format (Likert vs. semantic differential vs. VAS), item order, and context. The station reveals how subtle wording changes shift response distributions by 10-30% (e.g., 'forbid' vs. 'not allow' effects, Schwarz, 1999), how item order creates assimilation or contrast effects, and how scale labeling (numeric vs. verbal anchors) changes extreme responding. The player calibrates items to minimize acquiescence, social desirability, and reference group effects. Cross-cultural module: response scales that work in individualist cultures may fail in collectivist cultures due to moderacy bias and reference group effects (Heine et al., 2002; Uskul et al., 2013).

stimulus.research_question: Measuring subjective well-being among college students

levels: 'How satisfied are you with your life?'
'All things considered, how are things these days?'
scrubbable_parameters.effect: slight differences in mean (0.1-0.3 SD) but large differences in correlations with other constructs (Schwarz, 1999)
verbal anchors anchor interpretation and reduce extreme responding; numeric ranges without anchors increase extreme scores (Krosnick & Presser, 2010)

levels: global life satisfaction first vs. last
scrubbable_parameters.effect: global first ÔåÆ unaffected; global after specific items ÔåÆ contrast effect, correlation r decreases by 0.10-0.15 (Schwarz & Strack, 1999)
Chinese mean SWLS ~0.5 SD lower than US for same objective conditions; Japanese responses shift when primed with reference group norms (Heine et al., 2002)

title: The Online Lab: Running Experiments on the Internet
description: A dialogue simulation where the player takes on the role of a researcher recruiting participants online (MTurk, Prolific, social media) for a classic social psychology experiment. The player must decide on recruitment platform, sampling strategy, attention checks, dropout prevention, and technical implementation. Each decision produces a simulated outcome: data quality metrics (attention check pass rate, completion time distributions, dropout rate) and statistical power (effective N vs. nominal N). The player learns how online samples differ from lab samples (more diverse but lower attention), how to detect bots and careless responders, and how platform-specific norms affect generalizability. The final challenge: replicating a classic priming effect online and diagnosing why the effect might fail in the absence of lab control (e.g., participant environment variation, multitasking).

stimulus.replication_target: warmth-priming effect on helping behavior (original lab: d = 0.45, N = 60)

decisions.trade_offs: MTurk: low cost, attention issues, 2-5% bot rate. Prolific: higher data quality, higher cost per participant. Social media: more diverse but uncontrolled environment.

decisions.effect: no checks ÔåÆ 8-12% careless responding (Oppenheimer et al., 2009); IMC catches ~50% of inattentive participants
progress bar reduces dropout by 15%; bonus payment reduces by 25% (Zhou & Fishbach, 2016)
30% of online participants multitask; mobile participants have 25% lower attention check pass rate than desktop (Goodman et al., 2013)

stimulus.feedback: after each decision round, receive a data quality report and revised power analysis. Target: achieve attention check pass rate > 90% and achieve > 0.80 power for expected d = 0.30 (accounting for regressive shrinkage).

title: Beeper in Your Pocket: Designing an Experience Sampling Study
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player designs a full experience-sampling method (ESM) study. The player scrubs parameters like sampling schedule (random vs. fixed vs. event-contingent), number of signals per day (typical: 5-10), signal duration, retrospective recall window (momentary vs. end-of-day), and compensation structure. The station shows how each parameter affects compliance rates, data quality, participant burden, and the types of research questions addressable. Using real ESM studies as templatesÔÇödaily mood variation (Clark & Watson, 1988), racial discrimination experiences (Ong et al., 2009), creative idea production (Gable et al., 2019)ÔÇöthe player learns that momentary reports differ systematically from end-of-day reconstructions (Lucas et al., 2021; Sprecher, 1999), and that the choice of sampling strategy determines which research questions can be answered.

scrubbable_parameters.effect: random reduces anticipation bias; fixed allows systematic time-of-day analysis; event-contingent captures rare behaviors
8+ signals per day ÔåÆ compliance drops below 70% after day 3; 3-5 signals ÔåÆ 85%+ compliance through day 14 (Reis et al., 2000)
end-of-day reports show 25% lower variance, 0.15 higher mean rating for positive affect compared to momentary (Lucas et al., 2021)
14+ days needed for stable within-person correlations; > 7 days needed for weekly cycle coverage; compliance decays ~3% per week

research_questions: Do people feel happier after social interactions than alone? (random sampling, 5/day, 7 days)
Do creative insights occur more during exercise than during rest? (event-contingent + random, 14 days)
How does daily experience of discrimination predict end-of-day mood? (end-of-day reconstruction + random momentary, 21 days)

title: Sensing the Self: Building a Mobile Sensing Study
description: A boss battle where the player designs a mobile sensing study using smartphone and wearable sensor data. The player must select sensor types (GPS, accelerometer, Bluetooth, call/SMS logs, screen time, ambient audio), define features to extract (mobility entropy, step count, social interaction count, sleep duration), and address technical challenges (battery drain, data missingness, privacy, sampling frequency). Each decision affects the effective sample size and signal-to-noise ratio. Research cases include predicting GPA from smartphone data (SmartGPA; Wang et al., 2015), detecting depression from behavioral markers (Wang et al., 2018), and assessing first-generation student stress (Wang et al., 2022). The final boss: design a multimodal study combining sensing with ESM self-reports (Stachi et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2021) and achieve > 80% capture rate with < 15% battery drain per day.

boss_levels.research_goal: predict academic performance (GPA) from passive smartphone data
boss_levels.key_features: mobility entropy (GPS), study duration (screen), social interaction count (Bluetooth/call logs)
boss_levels.challenge: missing GPS data (20% when indoors): impute or exclude?

boss_levels.research_goal: detect depression onset from behavioral changes
boss_levels.key_features: reduced mobility, increased phone usage at night, decreased speech duration in ambient audio, irregular sleep
boss_levels.expected_accuracy: AUC = 0.82 (depression vs. control; Wang et al., 2018)
boss_levels.challenge: privacy: participant concern about ambient audio. Option: use audio features extracted on-device without sending raw audio to server

boss_levels.research_goal: integrate mobile sensing with ESM self-report (StudentLife; Wang et al., 2014)
sensors_available: all above + ESM prompts (5/day) + battery level + WiFi scans
boss_levels.challenge_final_boss: battery drain: continuous GPS + accelerometer + audio sampling consumes 25% battery/day. Solution: adaptive sampling (reduce GPS frequency when accelerometer shows stationary). Target: < 15% battery drain/day.

title: Words as Data: LIWC and Psychological Language Analysis
description: An audit file where the player uses Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC; Pennebaker et al., 2015) to analyze text samples and detect psychological states. The player reviews natural language samplesÔÇöpersonal essays, therapy transcripts, social media posts, love lettersÔÇöand must identify linguistic markers of depression (first-person singular pronouns, negative emotion words, absolutist words), deception (fewer first-person pronouns, fewer exclusive words), status (pronoun use patterns reflecting power dynamics), and relationship quality (we-talk vs. I-talk). The player learns that function words (pronouns, articles, prepositions) are more diagnostic than content words for psychological states, that word count correlates with extraversion, and that people are surprisingly poor at self-reporting their own language patterns (Ireland & Pennebaker, 2014).

text_indicators: elevated first-person singular (I, me, my): +40% vs. controls
case_files.benchmark: LIWC depression classification: AUC = 0.78, sensitivity 72%, specificity 71%
case_files.player_task: review transcript and flag linguistic depression markers; compute LIWC category scores

text_indicators: fewer first-person pronouns (I, me, my): -15% vs. truthful
case_files.benchmark: LIWC deception detection accuracy: 61% (slightly above chance; Pennebaker et al., 2003)
case_files.player_task: compare truthful vs. deceptive statement pairs; identify which linguistic features discriminate them

case_files.domain: relationship quality in couples' text messages
text_indicators: higher we-talk (we, our, us): +30% in satisfied vs. distressed couples
pronoun synchrony: conversation partners matching pronoun rates
case_files.benchmark: we-talk predicts relationship stability over 3-month follow-up, OR = 1.45 (Sillars et al., 1997)
case_files.player_task: rate relationship satisfaction from pronoun use patterns alone; compare to self-report

title: Coding the Stream: Designing a Behavioral Observation System
description: A dialogue simulation where the player builds a behavioral coding scheme from scratch. The player chooses a research question (e.g., 'Does power affect conversational dominance?') and must define coding units (events vs. time intervals), select coding categories (verbal vs. nonverbal: interruptions, gaze, gesture, body orientation), establish inter-rater reliability targets (Cohen's kappa > 0.70), and decide between real-time coding, video coding, and automated coding. The simulation shows a series of interaction clips and the player codes behavior into chosen categories, receiving kappa feedback against expert coders (Thorson & West). The player learns that overly narrow categories produce high reliability but low validity, overly broad categories do the opposite, and that behavioral observation reveals patterns invisible to self-report ÔÇö for example, people over-report their own interruptions by 40% compared to coded observation.

stimulus.research_question: Does power asymmetry affect nonverbal dominance displays in dyadic conversation?

coding_choices.reliability_tradeoff: event-based yields highest kappa (0.85) but misses duration; interval-based captures duration but lower kappa (0.72)
more categories ÔåÆ lower kappa per category (dilution effect); fewer categories risk missing power dynamics

coding_choices.trade_off: real-time = high ecological validity but low reliability; video = highest reliability but time-intensive (4:1 coding ratio); automated = high-speed but limited to well-defined behaviors

title: The IAT Lab: Automaticity, Implicit Measures, and the Attitude-Behavior Gap
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player takes the Implicit Association Test (IAT) and then manipulates its parameters to understand how it works. The player scrubs stimulus categories, trial order (compatible vs. incompatible blocks), inter-trial interval, response window, and scoring algorithm (D-score vs. simple difference). The station reveals how the IAT's D-score is influenced by: category salience, familiarity with stimuli, speed-accuracy trade-offs, and procedural variations. The player then compares their explicit (self-report) and implicit (IAT) attitude scores, learning about the attitude-behavior gap (Greenwald et al., 2009). Cross-cultural module: IAT effects differ by culture even when explicit attitudes do not, revealing differences in automatic associations shaped by different cultural environments (Gawronski & Bodenhausen, 2006). The final module addresses controversy: does the IAT predict discriminatory behavior, or mostly measure cultural knowledge?

player_actions: view personal D-score and interpretation (Greenwald et al., 2003 norms)

scrubbable_parameters.effect: abstract labels reduce IAT effect by d = 0.10-0.15 (Steffens & Plewe, 2001)
Pleasant/Unpleasant produces larger effects for the race IAT than Good/Bad (Gawronski et al., 2008)
order effects: compatible-first produces D-scores ~0.20 higher than incompatible-first (Nosek, Greenwald & Banaji, 2005)
D-score has highest internal consistency (alpha > 0.80) and smallest order effects; raw RT difference noisier

stimulus.debriefing: IAT predicts behavior best in uncontrolled, low-effort settings; explicit measures predict best in high-self-awareness settings (Dovidio et al., 2002)

title: Hormones and Behavior: Social Neuroendocrinology Methods
description: An audit file reviewing the methodological challenges of studying hormone-behavior links in social psychology. The player examines case studies of cortisol (stress) and testosterone (dominance) research, learning about: salivary collection protocols (time of day, compliance, contamination), circadian rhythms (typical cortisol peak at 30 min post-waking, trough at midnight), hormonal assays (ELISA vs. LC-MS/MS), and the challenge of establishing directionality (does testosterone cause dominance, or does dominance increase testosterone?). Case files include: the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993), the hormone-competition link in sports (Mendes, 2009), and the winner effect in competitive tasks. The player must identify confounds that threaten internal validity: diurnal variation, baseline differences, reactivity to collection, and the reciprocal coupling of psychological and hormonal processes.

case_file_1.title: Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) ÔÇö cortisol reactivity
case_file_1.protocol: 5-min speech + 5-min mental arithmetic before evaluative audience
case_file_1.expected_cortisol_response: peak at 20-30 min post-stressor, 2-3x baseline, return to baseline by 60 min
confounds_to_identify: sampling time: afternoon cortisol lower than morning, smaller response window in PM
oral contraceptive use: blunts cortisol response, effect size d = 0.35
smoking: elevates baseline cortisol, reduces reactivity
collection compliance: participants must abstain from eating/drinking/caffeine 60 min prior

case_file_2.title: Testosterone and dominance behavior
case_file_2.finding: higher testosterone correlates with dominance behavior in competitive tasks (r = 0.20-0.30)
case_file_2.directionality_question: does testosterone cause dominant behavior, or does winning a competition increase testosterone?
case_file_2.evidence: Winner effect: testosterone rises in winners and falls in losers after competitive tasks, regardless of baseline (Archer, 2006). Supports bidirectional model.
confounds_to_identify: baseline differences in T vary by time of day (AM peak), age (declines after 30), body mass index
competitive context priming: T measured in lab vs. field shows different effect sizes
measurement method: salivary T vs. serum T correlate r = 0.60-0.80, not interchangeable

title: Scale Construction: From Items to Latent Variables
description: A matrix exercise where the player builds a psychological scale from item pool to final validated instrument. The player starts with a target construct (e.g., 'gratitude') and a pool of candidate items. They must select items based on content validity, examine inter-item correlations, compute reliability (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega), conduct exploratory then confirmatory factor analysis, test for differential item functioning across gender and culture, and finally produce a scale with alpha > 0.80, clear factor structure, and convergent/discriminant validity evidence. The matrix shows each decision's impact on psychometric properties. Cross-cultural module: scale items that work in one culture may show DIF in anotherÔÇöMG-CFA is essential for establishing measurement invariance before group comparisons (Revelle & Garner; Little, 1997).

stimulus.construct: gratitude (dispositional tendency to notice and appreciate positive aspects of life)

item_pool.item: I have so much to be thankful for.
I often feel grateful for the small things in life.
Long, long ago, I can still remember how that music used to make me smile.
When I see something beautiful, I stop to appreciate it.
I don't really think about what I'm grateful for.

player_tasks: select items with content validity > 3.5 and item-total r > 0.40 (reject item 3 and item 6)
compute Cronbach's alpha on retained items; target > 0.80
conduct EFA: expect 1 factor (gratitude), loadings > 0.50 on retained items
test CFA in independent sample: acceptable fit (CFI > 0.90, RMSEA < 0.08)
test gender invariance: metric invariance should hold (delta CFI < 0.01)
test cultural invariance: some items may show DIF in collectivist vs. individualist samples
validity_checks: convergent: correlate with life satisfaction (r > 0.30 expected)
discriminant: correlate with neuroticism (r < -0.20, not r > -0.70)

title: Causal Inference: Mediation Analysis and the Quest for Mechanisms
description: A boss battle where the player must establish causal mediation using the potential outcomes framework. The player tests whether an independent variable X affects a dependent variable Y through a mediator M. Challenges include: selecting the correct mediator based on theory, establishing temporal precedence (X before M before Y), ruling out confounding in the M-Y relationship, handling measurement error in the mediator (which biases indirect effects), and choosing between Baron & Kenny (1986) causal steps, the Sobel test, and bootstrapped confidence intervals for the indirect effect (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). The final boss: a serial mediation model with two mediators in sequence, using sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding (Montoya, 2023; Imai, Keele & Tingley, 2010). The player must correctly specify the model, test the indirect effect, and argue whether the causal identification assumptions are plausible.

boss_levels.research_question: Does power reduce perspective-taking? X = power prime, M = reduced attentional focus on others, Y = perspective-taking accuracy
boss_levels.model: single mediator, parallel design (X randomly assigned)
requirements: X must precede M (temporal order: prime ÔåÆ measure attention ÔåÆ measure perspective-taking)
M-Y relationship must be unconfounded (need measured covariates to reduce omitted variable bias)
report bootstrapped 95% CI for ab indirect effect (5000 resamples)
if CI excludes zero, mediation is supported at alpha = 0.05
boss_levels.win_condition: detect significant indirect effect (CI excludes 0) and rule out reverse causation (X ÔåÆ Y ÔåÆ M)

boss_levels.research_question: Does social rejection lead to aggression through angry rumination? X = rejection vs. acceptance, M1 = angry rumination, M2 = hostile intent attribution, Y = aggressive behavior
boss_levels.model: serial mediation: X ÔåÆ M1 ÔåÆ M2 ÔåÆ Y (all continuous variables)
requirements: M1 must precede M2 (rumination measured before hostile attribution)
test specific indirect effect (a1 * d21 * b2) using bootstrapped CI
compare specific indirect effect against total indirect effect (proportion mediated)
run sensitivity analysis (Imai et al., 2010): how large would unmeasured confound have to be to invalidate the mediated effect?
boss_levels.win_condition: significant serial indirect effect + sensitivity analysis shows confound would need rho > 0.30 with both M2 and Y to eliminate indirect effect

title: Methods as Muse: Designing a Research Program
description: A dialogue simulation where the player acts as a grad student designing their first independent research program. They consult three senior methodologists, each advocating a different approach: careful experimental control ('internal validity first'), naturalistic observation ('external validity is paramount'), and computational modeling ('formalize your theory mathematically'). The player must weigh each advisor's arguments while reading about the methodological pluralism championed by the handbook editors (Reis, West & Judd). Each design choice shifts resources (time, budget, sample size) and validity trade-offs. The simulation teaches that 'methods open the door to questions' and that the best research programs toggle between theory refinement and method choice iteratively.

stimulus.research_interest: how social rejection affects prosocial behavior

advisors.name: Dr. Rigor
advisors.approach: lab experiment: cyberball rejection + dictator game giving

advisors.name: Prof. Naturalist
advisors.approach: field study: daily-diary ESM tracking rejection events and helping acts

advisors.name: Dr. Modeler
advisors.approach: computational model: agent-based simulation of rejection ÔåÆ compensation dynamics

stimulus.player_task: allocate 100 'research units' across internal validity, external validity, and construct validity. The distribution determines which types of claims the project can support.

title: The Romance File: Epistemic Foundations of Method
description: An audit file where the player traces the intellectual lineage of common research methods back to their philosophical origins. Mahzarin Banaji's chapter frames method as 'romance' ÔÇö the mystery and excitement of systematic discovery. The player reviews method case files (experiment, survey, observation, computational modeling) and must identify which epistemological tradition each descends from: Aristotelian logic and systematic observation, Bacon's Novum Organum (empiricism and induction), Popperian falsification, Kuhn's paradigm shifts, or the Bayesian revolution. Each case highlights how methodological assumptions shape what counts as evidence. The final file asks the player to reflect: Do our methods merely test theories, or do they also constrain what theories we can imagine?

case_files.epistemic_root: Mill's methods of difference (1843); Fisher's randomization (1935)
case_files.assumption: comparison of otherwise identical conditions reveals causation

case_files.epistemic_root: Spearman's latent variable model (1904); factor analysis
case_files.assumption: unobservable constructs can be measured through multiple observable indicators

case_files.epistemic_root: Fisher's combination of p-values (1932); Glass's effect size (1976)
case_files.assumption: systematic integration across studies yields more truth than any single study

case_files.epistemic_root: Newell & Simon's physical symbol system (1976); Marr's levels of analysis (1982)
case_files.assumption: formalizing a theory forces precision and reveals hidden predictions

stimulus.final_prompt: Banaji argues that 'science reveals the nature of reality independently of whatever we may think or feel about it.' But methods themselves are human inventions. Do methods discover reality or construct it?

title: The IRB Simulation: Ethical Decision-Making in Research
description: A dialogue simulation where the player serves on an Institutional Review Board (IRB) reviewing four research protocols: a partial-replication of Milgram's obedience study, a deception-based experiment on intergroup bias, a mobile sensing study collecting passive GPS/location data, and a big-data project using public social media posts. For each protocol, the player must apply the Belmont principles (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) and decide approve/modify/reject (Crandall, Giner-Sorolla & Biernat). The simulation teaches the historical lessons: Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972), Nazi medical experiments (Nuremberg Code, 1947), Milgram (1963), and Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment (1971)ÔÇöeach of which shaped modern ethics codes. The player learns that ethical issues now extend beyond participant treatment to include data handling, open science practices, and equitable research partnerships.

protocols.title: Obedience revisited (partial Milgram replication)
protocols.special_issues: participants believe they are delivering real shocks; need for immediate debriefing + follow-up mental health screening
protocols.history: Milgram (1963): 14/40 showed uncontrollable seizures; led to requirement for debriefing

protocols.title: Implicit bias intervention (deception about partner race)
protocols.special_issues: deception essential for hypothesis; community consultation recommended; need for active debriefing that educates about implicit bias
protocols.history: Belmont report (1978): respect for persons requires informed consent; deception allowed only if: (a) essential, (b) no feasible alternative, (c) debriefing provided

protocols.title: Mobile sensing of mood via phone GPS + accelerometer
protocols.special_issues: continuous location tracking; data security; participant awareness of passive monitoring; plans for data breach response
protocols.history: new ethical frontier: informed consent must cover passive data collection; participants may not anticipate GPS tracking granularity

protocols.title: Public Twitter data analysis (no interaction)
protocols.special_issues: public data vs. reasonable expectation of privacy; re-identification risk; whether terms of service adequately protect users
protocols.history: Belmont: justice requires equitable distribution of research burdens/b benefits; are social media datasets biased toward certain populations?

title: Building the Diverse Team: Interdisciplinary Collaboration
description: A dialogue simulation where the player assembles a research team for a complex project (understanding how structural inequality affects health outcomes). The player must recruit members from different disciplines (psychology, sociology, public health, computer science, economics) and demographic backgrounds, managing the challenges of interdisciplinary collaboration: different vocabularies, conflicting standards of evidence, varying publication norms, and power dynamics. Drawing on Tepper & Lewis's framework, the simulation shows that diversity in team composition improves research question generation and methodological creativity ÔÇö but only if team processes are structured to ensure all voices are heard. The player earns 'discovery points' for broad framing and 'precision points' for rigorous methods; the best teams balance both.

stimulus.research_problem: How do neighborhood environments shape mental health disparities?
challenges: psychology wants tightly controlled experiments; sociology wants ethnographic observation. How to reconcile?
CS wants big data and ML models; clinical wants validated self-report measures. How to integrate?
Community advocate insists research must benefit the community, not just extract data. How to operationalize?
Differential status: tenured professors and clinicians may dominate conversations over junior researchers and advocates. How to structure meetings for equity?

title: Quasi-Experimental Design Lab: Regression Discontinuity and Interrupted Time Series
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player learns to design quasi-experiments when random assignment is impossible. Using Fabrigar, Vaughan-Johnston & Wegener's framework, the player explores two core designs: (1) Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) ÔÇö assignment is based on a cutoff on a continuous variable (e.g., minimum GPA for scholarship); the player scrubs the cutoff value, the functional form (linear vs. curvilinear), and the bandwidth, observing how each choice affects the estimated treatment effect. (2) Interrupted Time Series (ITS) ÔÇö the player scrubs the intervention point, seasonality parameters, and comparison series (relevant vs. irrelevant outcome), learning how A-B, A-B-A, and multiple-baseline designs control for history threats. The player analyzes real-data-inspired cases: effect of a minimum-wage increase on employment, effect of a policy intervention on COVID-19 transmission, and effect of academic probation on student performance.

designs.name: Regression Discontinuity
validity_threats: sorting around cutoff (participants manipulate assignment variable)
designs.player_actions: scrub polynomial order (1-3), bandwidth (┬▒ 0.5 SD, ┬▒ 1 SD, ┬▒ 2 SD), and see how estimated tau changes

designs.name: Interrupted Time Series
designs.player_actions: scrub intervention point, add seasonality control, add comparison series (relevant vs. irrelevant outcome)

example_cases: minimum wage increase (state-level, cutpoint at $15/hour): does employment drop at the cutoff?
academic probation policy (GPA cutoff = 2.0): does removal of financial aid affect subsequent GPA?

title: Field Research: Conducting Experiments in the Wild
description: A boss battle where the player must design and execute a field experiment testing the effect of social norm nudges on real-world behavior. The player chooses from field settings (cafeteria, park, neighborhood, online platform), selects the intervention delivery mechanism (signage, interpersonal request, ambient design), and decides on measurement (covert observation, trace measures, administrative data). Each choice introduces practical threats: contamination between conditions (the 'cafeteria problem' where treatment spreads via social talk), measurement reactivity (the 'Hawthorne effect'), and loss of experimental control (weather, third variables). The player must achieve > 80% treatment fidelity while keeping the experiment invisible to participants (Wu & Littman's emphasis on naturalistic behavioral observation). The final boss: a field experiment on reducing energy consumption through descriptive vs. injunctive social norms, where the player must handle seasonality, metering errors, and neighbor-to-neighbor spillover.

boss_levels.research_question: Do descriptive norms (what others do) increase cafeteria vegetable consumption?
boss_levels.intervention: sign: '9 out of 10 students choose a vegetable with their meal'
threats: contamination: students talk to each other about signs
measurement: tray waste observation is time-intensive
reactivity: kitchen staff may change vegetable preparation
boss_levels.win_condition: achieve > 80% fidelity (sign visible to 80% of target population) with unobtrusive measurement

boss_levels.research_question: Do injunctive norms (what should be done) reduce littering in parks?
boss_levels.intervention: sign with frowning face + 'Don't be a litterbug ÔÇö our park deserves better'
threats: weather affects park attendance and littering behavior
confound: park ranger presence varies across days
measurement: litter count requires systematic daily collection
boss_levels.win_condition: replicate the 15% litter reduction found in Cialdini et al. (1990) while controlling for weather covariates

boss_levels.boss_round: social norms and household energy consumption
boss_levels.intervention: door-hanger with descriptive norm (your kWh vs. neighbors) vs. injunctive norm (smiley/frowny face)
threats: metering errors: smart meter data gaps
seasonality: summer AC vs. winter heating confounds
boss_levels.win_condition: replicate Schultz et al. (2007) effect: descriptive norm alone reduces consumption 4%, but boomerang effect in low-consumers; injunctive norm eliminates boomerang. Achieve valid causal inference despite no random assignment of houses.

title: Digital Footprints: Mining Social Media for Psychological Insight
description: A dialogue simulation where the player analyzes digital footprints from simulated Facebook profiles to predict personality, political orientation, and life satisfaction. Kosinski's chapter shows that digital records created during everyday online activities provide a rich window into the human mind. The player extracts features from Facebook Likes, status updates, profile pictures, and friend networks, and trains a model to predict a target person's traits. Key findings from real research: 10 Likes predict a person's traits better than a colleague's rating (r = 0.39); 300 Likes predict better than a spouse (r = 0.57; Kosinski et al., 2013). The player then navigates the ethical tightrope: these same methods can be used for beneficial personalization or manipulative targeting (Cambridge Analytica case). The simulation ends with a decision: publish the prediction model (high-impact, privacy risk) or withhold it (ethical, less impact).

stimulus.data_source: Facebook Likes, status text, friend network, demographics (simulated) for hypothetical participant 'Alex'

prediction_targets.digital_features: number of friends, Like count for party-themed pages, status length, use of positive emotional language
Likes for political pages, use of moral foundation language
sentiment analysis of status updates, Like count for inspirational pages, photo sentiment

stimulus.ethics_dilemma: Your prediction model is 90% accurate for sexual orientation (Wang & Kosinski, 2018). A political campaign offers $2M to target undecided voters. Do you sell the model?

title: fMRI Lab: Univariate and Multivariate Approaches
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player analyzes fMRI data using both traditional univariate (voxel-wise GLM) and modern multivariate (MVPA, RSA) approaches (Chavez, Cunningham & Berkman). The player scrubs across analysis methods: standard univariate contrasts (face > house activation in FFA), representational similarity analysis (RSA ÔÇö comparing neural pattern similarity to behavioral similarity), and multivariate decoding (training a classifier to predict mental states from activation patterns). The player learns key trade-offs: univariate reveals WHERE but not HOW information is represented; multivariate reveals information content at the cost of spatial specificity; RSA bridges brain and behavior at the level of representational structure. Each choice affects statistical power and multiple comparison correction (cluster-level FWE vs. FDR vs. Bayesian approaches).

analysis_methods.name: Univariate GLM
analysis_methods.key_concept: contrasts: face > house in FFA (fusiform face area)

analysis_methods.name: Multivariate Pattern Analysis (MVPA)
analysis_methods.question_type: WHAT information is represented in a region?
analysis_methods.key_concept: linear classifiers (SVM) decode mental states from voxel patterns

analysis_methods.name: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)
analysis_methods.key_concept: correlate neural similarity matrices with behavioral/theoretical similarity matrices

title: Psychometric Forensics: Item Bias, DIF, and Measurement Fairness
description: An audit file where the player investigates whether a psychological scale measures the same construct across groups. Using Shrout & Mogami's advanced psychometric framework, the player reviews case files of scales shown to contain differential item functioning (DIF): a cognitive ability test with gender bias in math word problems (tool context), a political orientation scale with cultural DIF, and a psychopathology scale with age-based DIF. The player must detect DIF using multiple-group CFA (testing configural ÔåÆ metric ÔåÆ scalar invariance) and IRT-based likelihood ratio tests. The final case asks whether to remove DIF items (improving fairness but changing construct coverage) or retain them (maintaining content validity but biasing comparisons).

case_files.example_item: If John needs 30 feet of fencing for a garden that is 10 ft x 5 ft, and his friend Maria needs help measuring ÔÇö
case_files.DIF_source: gender-based stereotype activation (tool context favors boys; girls of equal ability score lower on items with mechanical/construction framing)
case_files.detection_method: IRT likelihood ratio test: item has significant DIF (chi-square = 14.2, p < 0.01)
case_files.decision: reword item to remove mechanical context, retest DIF

case_files.example_item: The family is the foundation of a moral society
case_files.DIF_source: cultural DIF: item loads higher for US respondents than Japanese respondents (reference group effect on 'family' as a moral unit)
case_files.detection_method: MG-CFA: metric invariance fails (delta CFI = 0.03 > 0.01); item loading = 0.65 (US) vs. 0.38 (Japan)
case_files.decision: consider cross-cultural adaptation vs. removing item from cross-cultural comparisons

case_files.item_example: Thoughts that you would be better off dead
case_files.DIF_source: age DIF: endorsement rate is same but item threshold (severity) differs ÔÇö older adults endorse at lower depression severity levels
case_files.detection_method: graded response IRT model: item threshold parameters differ by age (d = 0.4 SD)
case_files.decision: use age-specific cutoffs for clinical diagnosis; retain item for dimensional research

title: Longitudinal Modeling: Multilevel Growth Curves
description: A boss battle where the player builds a multilevel model (MLM) for longitudinal data. Using Gordon & Thorson's framework, the player specifies the model level by level: Level 1 (within-person change over time ÔÇö time metric, linear vs. quadratic vs. cubic slope), Level 2 (between-person predictors of change ÔÇö sex, initial status, treatment group), and error covariance structure (compound symmetry, autoregressive, unstructured). The 'boss' is a series of increasingly complex longitudinal research questions: (1) Does daily stress predict mood? (simple 2-level daily diary), (2) Does a mindfulness intervention reduce stress over 8 weeks? (3-level: time within person within group), (3) Does couple-level conflict predict individual depression over 2 years? (crossed random effects: partners nested in couples and in measurement occasions). Each correct specification yields higher power; each misspecification inflates Type I error.

boss_levels.research_question: Does daily stress predict daily mood?
boss_levels.power_note: effective N = participants ├ù days / design effect; 30 days ICC = 0.50 ÔåÆ effective N Ôëê 65

boss_levels.research_question: Does mindfulness reduce stress more than active control over 8 weeks?
boss_levels.data_structure: 9 waves ├ù 40 participants per group ├ù 2 groups = 720 observations
boss_levels.win_condition: detect significant group ├ù time interaction with optimal power

boss_levels.research_question: Do couples' conflict-resolution behaviors predict depression trajectories?
boss_levels.data_structure: 4 waves ├ù 200 couples = 1600 observations, crossed random effects
boss_levels.recommended_model: APIM growth model with crossed partner random effects (Kenny et al., Ch23)
challenges: actor vs. partner effects of conflict on depression slope
boss_levels.win_condition: correctly specify crossed random effects (partner 1 and partner 2 random intercepts correlated) and separate actor from partner effects

title: Dyadic Data: The Actor-Partner Interdependence Model
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player analyzes data from dyads (romantic couples, parent-child, friends, strangers) using the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) from Kenny, Ackerman & Kashy. The player scrubs key parameters: dyadic distinction (distinguishable vs. indistinguishable dyads), effect sizes (actor effect, partner effect), and nonindependence (Pearson r between partners' outcomes). The station shows how the standard regression assumption of independence fails for dyadic data (partners' outcomes are correlated, biasing SEs). The player must select the correct analysis: APIM with SEM (for distinguishable dyads with different actor and partner effects for each role) vs. pooled APIM (for indistinguishable dyads, constrained actor and partner effects). The final module introduces the common fate model (dyad-level outcome) vs. mutual influence model (bidirectional partner effects), teaching when each is appropriate.

stimulus.research_scenario: Do partner support behaviors predict individual well-being in couples?
stimulus.data_structure: 200 couples, each partner reports: perceived support received (X) and well-being (Y)

apim_parameters.definition: effect of my own support on my own well-being
effect of my partner's support on my well-being

apim_parameters.analysis: distinguishable ÔåÆ unconstrained actor/partner effects per role; indistinguishable ÔåÆ pooled effects

special_cases.when_to_use: both partners share a common cause (e.g., same environment)
special_cases.why: outcomes determined by dyad-level factor, not individual partner effects

special_cases.when_to_use: partners influence each other's outcomes reciprocally
special_cases.why: X1 ÔåÆ Y2 and X2 ÔåÆ Y1 simultaneously; requires instrumental variables or longitudinal data

title: Random Factors: Generalizing Beyond the Study
description: A dialogue simulation where the player must decide whether their research findings generalize beyond their specific materials, participants, and settings. Judd & Kenny's chapter argues that stimuli (words, faces, scenarios) and participants are both random factors ÔÇö failing to treat them as such artificially inflates Type I error (the 'language-as-fixed-effect fallacy', Clark, 1973). The player designs a study testing whether warm vs. neutral words are recalled better. They must choose: participant-only random effects (treating words as fixed) vs. crossed random effects (both participants and words as random). The simulation runs both analyses on the same data, showing the crossed model produces larger SEs and wider CIs, but correct Type I error. The player learns that the appropriate generalization space includes both participant population AND stimulus population, and that ignoring stimulus variability inflates false-positive rates by 2-5x.

stimulus.study_design: 32 participants read 40 words (20 warm, 20 neutral) and complete recall test

analysis_options.generalization_claim: results generalize to new participants, but not new words
results generalize to new participants AND new words

mini_meta_lesson: When materials are sampled, they are a random factor
Not treating them as such leads to anti-conservative p-values (Clark, 1973)
Minimal generalization space = participants + materials + situations
Quasi-F ratios or bootstrapping can estimate the correct SE (Judd, Westfall & Kenny, 2012)

title: Modeling the Mind: Formal Computational Approaches
description: A dialogue simulation where the player compares verbal theory vs. formal computational model for explaining a classic social-psychological phenomenon: cognitive dissonance. Klauer's chapter argues that verbal theories are often vague, unfalsifiable, or incomplete, while formal models force precision and reveal hidden predictions. The player defines: (1) a verbal theory of dissonance ('inconsistency between attitudes causes discomfort, which motivates attitude change'), (2) a connectionist model (Hopfield network settling into consistent activation patterns), and (3) a Bayesian model (belief updating under prior expectations). The player then tests each 'theory' against simulated data from Festinger & Carlsmith's (1959) $1/$20 paradigm. The Bayesian model best fits the data pattern and generates a novel prediction (disconfirmed in replication, leading to model revision). The simulation teaches that 'the model is the theory' and that the goal is not just to fit data but to generate testable predictions that advance the field.

models.predictions: insufficient justification ÔåÆ larger attitude change
models.falsifiability: low ÔÇö can always add post-hoc parameters

models.predictions: attitude nodes settle into consistent states; inconsistency = energy; stronger interference = more energy = more change
models.falsifiability: medium ÔÇö free parameters (learning rate, temperature)

models.predictions: posterior attitude = weighted average of prior and observed behavior; insufficient justification ÔåÆ less weight on behavior ÔåÆ less attitude change vs. paid condition
models.falsifiability: high ÔÇö priors can be independently measured
models.fit_to_data: best fit; predicts boundary condition: no dissonance when behavior is coerced beyond credibility

title: Meta-Analysis Lab: Combining Effect Sizes, Forest Plots, and Publication Bias
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player conducts a simulated meta-analysis of 20 studies on the effect of stereotype threat on women's math performance. Using Hall & Miller's framework, the player selects the effect size metric (Cohen's d vs. Hedges' g vs. Fisher's z), chooses the model (fixed vs. random effects), and extracts effect sizes from each study. The station computes the weighted mean effect, creates a forest plot with confidence intervals, and estimates heterogeneity (Q-statistic, I┬▓, tau┬▓). The player then scrubs through publication bias detection methods: funnel plot (asymmetry = bias), Egger's regression (significant intercept = bias), trim-and-fill (estimated number of missing studies), and p-curve analysis (distribution of significant p-values). The final module teaches that random-effects meta-analysis is almost always appropriate (due to heterogeneity of irrelevancies, Kenny & Judd, 2019) and that forest plots should be read as distributions of effects, not as binary 'exists/doesn't exist' verdicts.

stimulus.simulated_dataset: stereotype threat effect on female math performance (20 studies, N range 40-200)

meta_analysis_steps.action: extract d or compute from means/SDs for each study
meta_analysis_steps.result: vector of 20 effect sizes (range: -0.15 to 1.20, mean = 0.42)
Q = 67.8, df = 19, p < 0.001; I┬▓ = 72%; suggests real variability beyond sampling error
asymmetric: smaller studies show larger effects; Egger's test: t = 2.84, p = 0.01
right-skewed (evidential value present); 33% of p-values > 0.05 (adequate power)
